findings.finding: My current finding is that the problem reduces to solving a linear system over the integers: for a given α supported on {0,…,8}, we must find an integer sequence γ (the time‑reversal of β) such that the convolution (α⋆γ)(n)=1 for exactly two distinct n=k,l and 0 elsewhere. This is equivalent to requiring that the 9×m matrix with entries α(t) (shifted appropriately) has a column‑space containing the two‑spike vector. Thus the existence of γ depends only on the support pattern of α, not on the magnitudes of its entries. This suggests a finite search over support patterns of α (2^9−1 possibilities) to count those admitting such a γ.

My current finding is that the problem is equivalent to finding all integer polynomials  
\(A(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}a_i t^i\) for which there exists a Laurent polynomial \(G(t)=\sum_j g_j t^j\) with integer coefficients such that  
\(A(t)\,G(t)=t^k+t^l\) for some distinct integers \(k,l\).  
Thus a “shifty” \(\alpha\) corresponds exactly to a length‑9 polynomial that can be factored (over \(\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]\)) into a product giving a two‑term monomial sum. This reformulation turns the original convolution condition into a purely algebraic factorization problem.

My current finding is that the problem reduces to a polynomial equation: for a given sequence \(A(x)=\sum_{s=0}^{8}\alpha(s)x^s\) (a degree‑8 polynomial with integer coefficients), there must exist a Laurent polynomial \(\gamma(x)=\sum_t\gamma(t)x^t\) and distinct integers \(k,l\) such that  
\[
A(x)\,\gamma(x)=x^k+x^l .
\]  
Thus a “shifty” \(\alpha\) is exactly one whose polynomial \(A(x)\) divides a binomial \(x^k+x^l\) in \(\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\). This equivalence turns the combinatorial question into a factorisation problem in the ring of Laurent polynomials.

My current finding is that a shifty function α corresponds to a polynomial \(A(z)=\sum_{i=0}^8\alpha(i)z^i\) such that there exists a positive integer \(d\) with \((1+z^d)/A(z)\in\mathbb Z[z,z^{-1}]\). Equivalently, \(A(z)\) (up to a sign) must be a divisor of the binomial \(1+z^d\) in the Laurent polynomial ring. Thus the problem reduces to counting integer polynomials of degree ≤8 that divide some binomial \(1+z^d\). This links the count to the factorization of cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_{2d}(z)\) since \(1+z^d=\Phi_{2d}(z)\) when \(d\) is odd, and \(1+z^d=(1+z)(1-z+z^2-\dots+z^{d-1})\) when \(d\) is even.

My current finding is that the existence of β is equivalent to the polynomial factorisation  
\(A(x)C(x)=x^{k}+x^{l}=x^{k}(1+x^{d})\) with \(d=l-k\neq0\).  
Thus a shifty α corresponds exactly to an integer polynomial \(A(x)\) of degree ≤8 that divides \(x^{k}(1+x^{d})\) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\).  Hence the problem reduces to counting all such divisors \(A(x)\) (up to the shift \(k\)) that have support inside \(\{0,\dots,8\}\).

Equivalently, letting \(c=\min\{i:a_i\neq0\}\) and \(A_c(t)=t^{-c}A(t)\) (so \(A_c(0)\neq0\)), we need \(A_c(t)\mid(1+t^d)\) for some \(d>0\). Thus the problem reduces to counting all integer polynomials of degree ≤8 whose “core” \(A_c(t)\) is a divisor of some \(1+t^d\). Equivalently, there exist integers $m,d>0$ such that $x^mA(x)$ divides $1+x^d$ in $\mathbb Z[x]$.  This reduces the problem to counting all monic polynomials of degree ≤8 with constant term 1 that are factors of some binomial $1+x^d$.  (Any such factor must itself be a product of cyclotomic polynomials $\Phi_r(x)$ with $r\mid2d$ and $r\nmid d$.)

My current finding is that a shifty α corresponds exactly to an integer polynomial \(A(x)=\sum_{t=0}^{8}\alpha(t)x^t\) that divides a two‑term polynomial \(x^k+x^l\) (with \(k,l\ge0,\ k\ne l\)).  Equivalently, \(A(x)=x^aE(x)\) where \(0\le a\le8\) and \(E(x)\) is a divisor of \(1+x^d\) for some non‑zero integer \(d\).  Thus the problem reduces to counting all such divisors \(E(x)\) (with \(\deg E\le8-a\)) and all admissible shifts \(a\).  This shows the existence of β depends only on the factorisation of \(1+x^d\), not on the specific values of \(\alpha(t)\).

Thus the problem reduces to counting degree‑≤8 integer polynomials that are divisors (up to a monomial) of some \(1+t^d\). This is a finite combinatorial question that can be attacked by enumerating all such divisors.

This reduces the problem to a finite combinatorial enumeration of subsets of odd integers whose weighted totient sum fits the bound.

\[
N=\sum_{P\mid1+x^d,\;\deg P\le8}\!2(8-\deg P+1).
\]  
This reduces the problem to enumerating all divisors of binomials \(1+x^d\) of degree at most 8.
